title: Funes: Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own
hook: Your agent's reasoning from last Tuesday vanishes when the session ends. Funes indexes past sessions locally so an agent can recall its own prior decisions instead of being re-briefed.
key_points: Problem: context dies with the session, and switching machines or agents loses it entirely.
Funes normalizes agent traces, chunks them, embeds locally with pinned models, and stores them in a Lance dataset.
Retrieval combines vector and BM25 search with cross-encoder reranking and recency weighting.
Agents call a `recall` tool autonomously; humans can query the archive with `funes ask`.
Works across Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes — the archive is yours, not a vendor's.
On handoff-versus-recall benchmarks the authors report recall 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one task and 4x on the other, succeeding on both where compaction failed on one.
content_html: Every coding-agent session starts from nothing. Whatever the agent figured out last Tuesday — why you rejected an approach, what the tricky invariant was — is gone, and re-establishing it means either a hand-written handoff or letting the agent rediscover it. Corvoysier's Funes, released open-source by Hugging Face, treats that as a retrieval problem over your own history.
extra_html:
How it works

Funes ingests agent traces into a standard format, chunks them, embeds them locally with pinned models, and stores the result in a Lance dataset. Queries blend vector search with BM25, then apply cross-encoder reranking and recency weighting. Agents reach it through a recall tool they can invoke themselves mid-task; you can also query directly with funes ask. It works across Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes, so the archive survives switching agents or machines.

Why it matters

The post's handoff-versus-recall benchmarks report recall being 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one task and 4x on the other, while succeeding on both — where compaction-based approaches failed on one. That's the useful reframing: the alternative to targeted recall isn't free, it's the cost of writing and re-reading a summary of everything. Code is at github.com/huggingface/funes.

related.title: The Handoff Tax: Swapping Models Mid-Run in Coding Agents
related.hook: Escalating a struggling coding agent to a stronger model recovers less than half the quality gap while costing a premium. Downshifting, oddly, is the good deal.

related.title: Agent Memory Is a Dose, Not a Switch
related.hook: IBM Research tested how much extracted guideline memory to give an agent. The right amount depends on the model: strong ones absorb everything, weaker ones do better with curated retrieval.

flashcards.prompt: What does Funes retrieve over, and how?
flashcards.back_html: Chunked, locally embedded agent session traces in a Lance dataset — queried with hybrid vector plus BM25 search, cross-encoder reranking, and recency weighting.

flashcards.prompt: What advantage did recall show over a written handoff in the post's benchmarks?

choices.text: It was 8x cheaper on one task and 4x on the other, and succeeded on both
It was slower but produced more accurate summaries
It removed the need for the agent to read any source files

flashcards.explanation_html: Retrieving only the relevant slice of past reasoning beats paying to write and re-read a full handoff document — and compaction methods failed on one of the two tasks.

flashcards.prompt: Why does 'a memory you own' matter for agent memory specifically?
flashcards.back_html: The archive is local and portable across agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, Hermes), so your accumulated reasoning isn't locked to one vendor's session store.
